title: Ἕκτορος ἔγερσις
titleEn: Poseidon Yields, Apollo Rouses Hector — Iliad 15.184–280
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Poseidon, still furious at Zeus’s message, answers Iris: he is no subject of his brother, for the three sons of Cronus drew lots, and Zeus has only the heavens, while the earth and Olympus are common to all. Iris reminds him that minds can be turned and that the Erinyes follow the elder, and he gives way for now, though he warns that if Zeus spares Ilium he will make a lasting enemy of him. He leaves the army and plunges into the sea. Zeus then sends Apollo to Hector with the aegis, to rouse him and drive the Achaeans back to the ships. Apollo finds Hector sitting up, only just recovered from his wound, and tells him a helper has come from Ida. Hector runs forward like a horse that has broken its tether, and the Danaans, who had been pressing the Trojans like hunters after a stag, scatter like men met by a lion.

sentences.t: τὴν δὲ μέγ’ ὀχθήσας προσέφη κλυτὸς ἐννοσίγαιος·
sentences.tr: tēn de meg’ ochthēsas prosephē klytos ennosigaios·
sentences.l: Her, greatly vexed, addressed the famous earth-shaker:
sentences.i: Greatly troubled, the famous earth-shaker said to her:
sentences.n: τήν is Iris, who has just finished her message from Zeus, and the article stands as a pronoun, ‘her’. ὀχθήσας is the aorist participle of ὀχθέω ‘be vexed, troubled’, with μέγα ‘greatly’ as its adverb. κλυτὸς ἐννοσίγαιος ‘the famous earth-shaker’ is Poseidon, named only by his epithet; ἐννοσίγαιος and ἐνοσίχθων (205) both mean ‘earth-shaker’. The edition ends the line with a raised dot, and his speech starts in the next line.

sentences.t:
ὢ πόποι ἦ ῥ’ ἀγαθός περ ἐὼν ὑπέροπλον ἔειπεν
εἴ μ’ ὁμότιμον ἐόντα βίῃ ἀέκοντα καθέξει.
sentences.tr:
ō popoi ē rh’ agathos per eōn hyperoplon eeipen
ei m’ homotimon eonta biēi aekonta kathexei.
sentences.l:
“Ah, arrogantly has he spoken, good though he is,
if me, equal in honour, unwilling, by force he shall hold back.
sentences.i: “Ah, he has spoken arrogantly, good though he is, if he will hold me back by force, unwilling as I am, me who am his equal in honour.
sentences.n: ὢ πόποι is the exclamation ‘Ah’. ἦ ῥ’ is ἦ ῥα, ‘truly, indeed’. ἀγαθός περ ἐών is ‘good though he is’, with ἐών the Homeric participle (Attic ὤν); ἀγαθός here is ‘good’ in the sense of strong and able. ὑπέροπλον is the neuter accusative used as an adverb; it means ‘arrogantly’ and is kin to ὑπεροπλίη ‘arrogance’ (1.205), though the formation of the word is not clear. The conditional εἴ … καθέξει takes the future ‘he will hold back’ and gives the ground of the charge in the first line. ὁμότιμον ‘equal in honour’ and ἀέκοντα ‘unwilling’ are accusatives agreeing with με.

sentences.t:
τρεῖς γάρ τ’ ἐκ Κρόνου εἰμὲν ἀδελφεοὶ οὓς τέκετο Ῥέα
Ζεὺς καὶ ἐγώ, τρίτατος δ’ Ἀΐδης ἐνέροισιν ἀνάσσων.
sentences.tr:
treis gar t’ ek Kronou eimen adelpheoi hous teketo Rhea
Zeus kai egō, tritatos d’ Aïdēs eneroisin anassōn.
sentences.l:
For three are we from Cronus, brothers, whom Rhea bore,
Zeus and I, and third Hades, ruling among those below.
sentences.i: For we are three brothers, sons of Cronus, whom Rhea bore: Zeus and I, and Hades the third, who rules over those below.
sentences.n: εἰμέν is the Homeric ‘we are’ (Attic ἐσμέν). ἐκ Κρόνου ‘from Cronus’ says whose sons they are, and Rhea is their mother. τρίτατος is the epic by-form of τρίτος ‘third’. ἐνέροισιν ‘those below’ is the dative plural of ἔνεροι, the dead and the powers under the earth, so Hades rules ‘among’ them.

sentences.t: τριχθὰ δὲ πάντα δέδασται, ἕκαστος δ’ ἔμμορε τιμῆς·
sentences.tr: trichtha de panta dedastai, hekastos d’ emmore timēs·
sentences.l: And in three parts all has been divided, and each has a share of honour;
sentences.i: Everything has been divided in three, and each of us has his share of honour;
sentences.n: τριχθά is ‘in three parts’, as at 2.668. δέδασται is the perfect passive of δατέομαι ‘divide’: the division has been made and stands. ἔμμορε is the perfect of μείρομαι ‘receive one’s share’, here with the genitive τιμῆς ‘of honour’; the Odyssey has the same clause at 11.338.

sentences.t:
ἤτοι ἐγὼν ἔλαχον πολιὴν ἅλα ναιέμεν αἰεὶ
παλλομένων, Ἀΐδης δ’ ἔλαχε ζόφον ἠερόεντα,
sentences.tr:
ētoi egōn elachon poliēn hala naiemen aiei
pallomenōn, Aïdēs d’ elache zophon ēeroenta,
sentences.l:
I indeed obtained by lot the grey sea to dwell in always,
the lots being shaken, and Hades obtained by lot the misty gloom,
sentences.i: I drew the grey sea to live in for ever, when the lots were shaken, and Hades drew the misty gloom,
sentences.n: ἔλαχον is the aorist of λαγχάνω ‘obtain by lot’; ἔλαχε in 191 is its third person. παλλομένων is a genitive absolute ‘(the lots) being shaken’, the noun left unspoken, from πάλλω ‘shake’. πολιὴν ἅλα ‘the grey sea’: πολιός ‘grey’ is the colour of the sea. ναιέμεν is the epic infinitive of ναίω ‘dwell’. ζόφον ἠερόεντα ‘the misty gloom’ is the dark under the earth. The edition prints ἤτοι as one word.

sentences.t: Ζεὺς δ’ ἔλαχ’ οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἐν αἰθέρι καὶ νεφέλῃσι·
sentences.tr: Zeus d’ elach’ ouranon euryn en aitheri kai nephelēisi·
sentences.l: and Zeus obtained by lot the broad heaven in the aether and the clouds;
sentences.i: and Zeus drew the broad heaven in the bright upper air and the clouds;
sentences.n: Ζεὺς δ’ ἔλαχ’ continues the drawing of lots; ἔλαχ’ is ἔλαχε with its last vowel elided. οὐρανὸν εὐρύν ‘the broad heaven’, with ἐν αἰθέρι καὶ νεφέλῃσι ‘in the aether and the clouds’, the bright air above and the cloud beneath it. νεφέλῃσι is the dative plural of νεφέλη ‘cloud’.

sentences.t: γαῖα δ’ ἔτι ξυνὴ πάντων καὶ μακρὸς Ὄλυμπος.
sentences.tr: gaia d’ eti xynē pantōn kai makros Olympos.
sentences.l: and the earth is still common to all, and tall Olympus.
sentences.i: The earth is still common to all, and tall Olympus.
sentences.n: ξυνή is the old spelling of κοινή (ξυν- for συν-), ‘common’. ἔτι ‘still’ says that the earth, left out of the lots, remains shared. πάντων is the genitive ‘to all’; the Greek says ‘common of all’. μακρὸς Ὄλυμπος ‘tall Olympus’ keeps the house rendering of μακρός.

sentences.t:
τώ ῥα καὶ οὔ τι Διὸς βέομαι φρεσίν, ἀλλὰ ἕκηλος
καὶ κρατερός περ ἐὼν μενέτω τριτάτῃ ἐνὶ μοίρῃ.
sentences.tr:
tō rha kai ou ti Dios beomai phresin, alla hekēlos
kai krateros per eōn menetō tritatēi eni moirēi.
sentences.l:
Therefore I shall by no means live by the mind of Zeus; but at ease,
and strong though he is, let him stay in his third share.
sentences.i: So I will not live as Zeus thinks I should; let him, strong though he is, stay at ease in his own third share.
sentences.n: τώ is ‘therefore’ (the old instrumental of the article). βέομαι is the epic future of βιόω ‘I shall live’, and Διὸς φρεσίν is ‘by the mind of Zeus’, the dative of the thing one lives by. ἕκηλος ‘at ease’ goes with μενέτω, ‘let him stay’, whose subject is Zeus. κρατερός περ ἐών ‘strong though he is’. τριτάτῃ ἐνὶ μοίρῃ is ‘in the third share’, the share of the heavens. The edition prints ἀλλὰ ἕκηλος without elision.

sentences.t: χερσὶ δὲ μή τί με πάγχυ κακὸν ὣς δειδισσέσθω·
sentences.tr: chersi de mē ti me panchy kakon hōs deidissesthō·
sentences.l: and with his hands let him not at all, altogether, frighten me like a coward;
sentences.i: and let him not frighten me with his hands, as if I were a coward;
sentences.n: δειδισσέσθω is the third person middle imperative of δειδίσσομαι ‘frighten’, here with an active force: ‘let him not scare me’. μή τι … πάγχυ ‘not at all, altogether’; χερσί is ‘with his hands’, that is by force. κακὸν ὣς ‘like a coward’ (as at 2.190, ‘like a κακός’, a man without courage); the accusative agrees with με, since the verb here is active in force, ‘frighten me’.

sentences.t:
θυγατέρεσσιν γάρ τε καὶ υἱάσι βέλτερον εἴη
ἐκπάγλοις ἐπέεσσιν ἐνισσέμεν οὓς τέκεν αὐτός,
οἵ ἑθεν ὀτρύνοντος ἀκούσονται καὶ ἀνάγκῃ.
sentences.tr:
thygateressin gar te kai huiasi belteron eiē
ekpaglois epeessin enissemen hous teken autos,
hoi hethen otrynontos akousontai kai anankēi.
sentences.l:
For to daughters and sons it would be better
to rebuke with terrifying words those whom he himself begot,
who will listen to him as he urges, even under compulsion.”
sentences.i: It would be better for him to rebuke with terrifying words his own daughters and sons, whom he himself fathered; they will listen to his urging even under compulsion.”
sentences.n: θυγατέρεσσιν and υἱάσι are datives plural, ‘to daughters and sons’, the persons rebuked (the dative goes with ἐνισσέμεν). βέλτερον εἴη ‘it would be better’ is followed by the infinitive ἐνισσέμεν, an infinitive of ἐνίσσω ‘rebuke’, the same verb as ἐνίπτω, and ἐκπάγλοις ‘terrifying’ qualifies ἐπέεσσιν ‘words’. οὓς τέκεν αὐτός ‘whom he himself begot’ names the sons and daughters, with τέκεν the aorist of τίκτω used of a father. ἑθεν is ἕθεν ‘of him’. ἑθεν ὀτρύνοντος is ‘him urging’, the genitive of the person heard after ἀκούσονται ‘they will hear, heed’, with the participle agreeing; ἀνάγκῃ is ‘under compulsion’. Line 197 is metrically irregular as transmitted: the first syllable of θυγατέρεσσιν, short by nature, is lengthened to serve as the long of the first foot, and καὶ is shortened before υἱάσι. Poseidon’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα ποδήνεμος ὠκέα Ἶρις·
sentences.tr: ton d’ ēmeibet’ epeita podēnemos ōkea Iris·
sentences.l: Him then answered wind-footed, swift Iris:
sentences.i: Then Iris, wind-footed and swift, answered him:
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα ‘and him then answered’ is the common formula of reply; ἠμείβετο is the imperfect of ἀμείβομαι ‘answer’. ποδήνεμος ‘wind-footed’ and ὠκέα ‘swift’ are the stock epithets of Iris.

sentences.t:
οὕτω γὰρ δή τοι γαιήοχε κυανοχαῖτα
τόνδε φέρω Διὶ μῦθον ἀπηνέα τε κρατερόν τε,
sentences.tr:
houtō gar dē toi gaiēoche kyanochaita
tonde pherō Dii mython apēnea te krateron te,
sentences.l:
“Is it thus then, earth-holder, dark-haired one,
that I carry this word to Zeus, unkind and strong?
sentences.i: “Is it so, then, earth-holder, dark-haired one, that I am to carry this word to Zeus, unkind and strong?
sentences.n: The Greek has no question word: οὕτω γὰρ δή τοι … φέρω is a question by its tone, ‘is it thus then, that I carry…?’, and the edition’s comma after κρατερόν τε is read as the end of that question, which the next words complete with ‘or…’. γαιήοχε and κυανοχαῖτα are vocatives, ‘earth-holder’ and ‘dark-haired one’, Poseidon’s epithets used alone. ἀπηνέα is ‘unkind’, the Odyssey’s word for ἀπηνής; κρατερόν is ‘strong’.

sentences.t: ἦ τι μεταστρέψεις;
sentences.tr: ē ti metastrepseis;
sentences.l: Or will you turn at all?
sentences.i: Or will you change your mind at all?
sentences.n: ἦ here is ‘or’, giving the other half of the question begun above. μεταστρέψεις is the future of μεταστρέφω ‘turn about’, here ‘change one’s course’, and τι ‘at all’ is adverbial.

sentences.t: στρεπταὶ μέν τε φρένες ἐσθλῶν.
sentences.tr: streptai men te phrenes esthlōn.
sentences.l: Turnable are the wits of the good.
sentences.i: The minds of good men can be turned.
sentences.n: στρεπταί is ‘turnable’, from τρέπω, the same adjective Phoenix applies to the gods at 9.497. μέν τε marks it as a general truth. φρένες is the plural ‘wits, minds’ and ἐσθλῶν the genitive ‘of the good’.

sentences.t: οἶσθ’ ὡς πρεσβυτέροισιν Ἐρινύες αἰὲν ἕπονται.
sentences.tr: oisth’ hōs presbyteroisin Erinyes aien hepontai.
sentences.l: You know how the Erinyes always follow the elder.”
sentences.i: You know that the Erinyes always attend the elder.”
sentences.n: οἶσθ’ is οἶσθα ‘you know’, and ὡς ‘how, that’ introduces what is known. Ἐρινύες are avenging spirits; they punish wrongs done to the elder, here Zeus as the elder brother. πρεσβυτέροισιν is the dative plural of the comparative ‘elder’, and ἕπονται ‘follow’ takes the dative. Iris’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε Ποσειδάων ἐνοσίχθων·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ aute proseeipe Poseidaōn enosichthōn·
sentences.l: Her then in turn addressed Poseidon earth-shaker:
sentences.i: Then Poseidon earth-shaker spoke to her in turn:
sentences.n: τὴν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε ‘and her in turn addressed’ opens a reply, with αὖτε ‘in turn’ for the change of speaker; προσέειπε is the epic προσεῖπε, ‘spoke to’. Ποσειδάων ἐνοσίχθων ‘Poseidon earth-shaker’ is the Odyssey’s phrase; the Odyssey has the masculine line at 8.354.

sentences.t: Ἶρι θεὰ μάλα τοῦτο ἔπος κατὰ μοῖραν ἔειπες·
sentences.tr: Iri thea mala touto epos kata moiran eeipes·
sentences.l: “Iris, goddess, this word you have spoken very much according to what is fitting;
sentences.i: “Iris, goddess, you have spoken that word altogether as is fitting;
sentences.n: Ἶρι θεά is a vocative, ‘Iris, goddess’. κατὰ μοῖραν ‘according to what is fitting’ is the Odyssey’s phrase, and μάλα ‘very much’ strengthens it. ἔειπες is the unaugmented aorist of λέγω, ‘you have spoken’. The edition prints a raised dot at the end of the line.

sentences.t: ἐσθλὸν καὶ τὸ τέτυκται ὅτ’ ἄγγελος αἴσιμα εἰδῇ.
sentences.tr: esthlon kai to tetyktai hot’ angelos aisima eidēi.
sentences.l: good this too has been made, when a messenger knows what is fitting.
sentences.i: It is a good thing, too, when a messenger knows what is fitting.
sentences.n: ἐσθλόν ‘good’ is the predicate, and καὶ τό ‘this too’ is the subject, the fact that the messenger knows what is right. τέτυκται is the perfect passive of τεύχω ‘make’, here ‘has come to be, is’. ὅτ’ is ὅτε ‘when’, with εἰδῇ the subjunctive of οἶδα for a general case, and αἴσιμα ‘fitting things’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ τόδ’ αἰνὸν ἄχος κραδίην καὶ θυμὸν ἱκάνει
ὁππότ’ ἂν ἰσόμορον καὶ ὁμῇ πεπρωμένον αἴσῃ
νεικείειν ἐθέλῃσι χολωτοῖσιν ἐπέεσσιν.
sentences.tr:
alla tod’ ainon achos kradiēn kai thymon hikanei
hoppot’ an isomoron kai homēi peprōmenon aisēi
neikeiein ethelēisi cholōtoisin epeessin.
sentences.l:
But this fearsome grief reaches my heart and spirit
whenever one equal in share and fated by the same portion
someone wishes to revile with angry words.
sentences.i: But this fearsome grief comes upon my heart and spirit whenever someone wishes to revile with angry words one who has an equal share and is fated by the same lot.
sentences.n: Line 208 is the same line as 8.147; here it runs on into the next two lines. ὁππότ’ ἂν … ἐθέλῃσι is the subjunctive of a general case, ‘whenever one wishes’. The accusative ἰσόμορον καὶ ὁμῇ πεπρωμένον αἴσῃ ‘equal in share and fated by the same portion’ is the object of νεικείειν ‘revile’; πεπρωμένον is the perfect participle passive of πόρω ‘allot’, so ‘fated’. The one reviled is Poseidon himself, equal in share with Zeus; the subject of ἐθέλῃσι, Zeus, is not named. χολωτοῖσιν ‘angry’ qualifies ἐπέεσσιν.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἤτοι νῦν μέν κε νεμεσσηθεὶς ὑποείξω·
sentences.tr: all’ ētoi nyn men ke nemessētheis hypoeixō·
sentences.l: But truly, for now, having felt resentment, I shall yield;
sentences.i: But for now, though resentful, I will give way;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἤτοι νῦν μέν ‘but truly, for now’ sets the present yielding against the threat in the next line. νεμεσσηθείς is the aorist participle of νεμεσσάω ‘feel resentment’. ὑποείξω is the subjunctive (or future) of ὑπείκω ‘give way’, and with κε it states a firm intention.

sentences.t: ἄλλο δέ τοι ἐρέω, καὶ ἀπειλήσω τό γε θυμῷ·
sentences.tr: allo de toi ereō, kai apeilēsō to ge thymōi·
sentences.l: And another thing I will tell you, and I will threaten it, that at least, in my spirit;
sentences.i: But I will tell you one thing more, and this at least I threaten in my spirit;
sentences.n: ἄλλο … ἐρέω ‘I will tell another thing’. ἐρέω is the future of λέγω. τοι is σοι ‘to you’. ἀπειλήσω is the future of ἀπειλέω ‘threaten’, with τό γε ‘this at least’ as its object. θυμῷ is ‘in my spirit’; the Greek does not say whether the threat is felt only inwardly or is meant in earnest.

sentences.t:
αἴ κεν ἄνευ ἐμέθεν καὶ Ἀθηναίης ἀγελείης
Ἥρης Ἑρμείω τε καὶ Ἡφαίστοιο ἄνακτος
Ἰλίου αἰπεινῆς πεφιδήσεται,
sentences.tr:
ai ken aneu emethen kai Athēnaiēs ageleiēs
Hērēs Hermeiō te kai Hēphaistoio anaktos
Iliou aipeinēs pephidēsetai,
sentences.i: if, without me, Athena the driver of spoil, Hera, Hermes and lord Hephaestus, he spares steep Ilios,
sentences.n: The protasis αἴ κεν … πεφιδήσεται is ‘if he shall spare’. ἄνευ ‘without’ governs five genitives: ἐμέθεν (= ἐμοῦ), Ἀθηναίης ἀγελείης, Ἥρης, Ἑρμείω (= Ἑρμοῦ) and Ἡφαίστοιο ἄνακτος; the list is joined by καὶ and τε … καὶ. ἀγελείης is ‘spoil-driver’, a word whose sense is not certain (ἄγω + λεία ‘booty’, as at 4.128). Ἰλίου αἰπεινῆς is the genitive after πεφιδήσεται (φείδομαι ‘spare’, which takes the genitive), and αἰπεινῆς ‘steep’ is the word for Ilios elsewhere.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἐθελήσει
ἐκπέρσαι, δοῦναι δὲ μέγα κράτος Ἀργείοισιν,
sentences.tr:
oud’ ethelēsei
ekpersai, dounai de mega kratos Argeioisin,
sentences.l:
and will not be willing
to sack-utterly, and to give great strength to the Argives,
sentences.i: and will not be willing to sack it, but to give the Argives great strength,
sentences.n: οὐδ’ ἐθελήσει ‘nor will he be willing’ goes with the two infinitives, ἐκπέρσαι ‘to sack utterly’ and δοῦναι ‘to give’. κράτος keeps ‘strength’ (1.509), which may include the upper hand. Ἀργείοισιν is the epic dative plural, ‘to the Argives’. The Greek protasis is still open, and its main clause comes in the next line.

sentences.t: ἴστω τοῦθ’ ὅτι νῶϊν ἀνήκεστος χόλος ἔσται.
sentences.tr: istō touth’ hoti nōïn anēkestos cholos estai.
sentences.l: let him know this, that for the two of us an incurable anger will exist.”
sentences.i: let him know this: between the two of us there will be an incurable anger.”
sentences.n: ἴστω is the third person imperative of οἶδα ‘let him know’. νῶϊν is the dual dative ‘for us two’, Poseidon and Zeus. ἀνήκεστος is ‘incurable’, literally ‘not to be healed’, from ἀκέομαι ‘heal’ with the negative prefix. χόλος keeps ‘anger’. Poseidon’s speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν λίπε λαὸν Ἀχαιϊκὸν ἐννοσίγαιος,
δῦνε δὲ πόντον ἰών,
sentences.tr:
hōs eipōn lipe laon Achaiïkon ennosigaios,
dyne de ponton iōn,
sentences.l:
So having spoken, he left the Achaean host, the earth-shaker,
and entered the sea, going;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the earth-shaker left the Achaean host and went down into the sea,
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών ‘so having spoken’ closes the speech. Ἀχαιϊκόν is the adjective ‘Achaean’, with the diaeresis as the edition prints it. ἐννοσίγαιος ‘the earth-shaker’ is Poseidon, named by his epithet alone. δῦνε is an unaugmented past form of δύνω (δύω) ‘enter, sink into’, and the participle ἰών ‘going’ shows how he went. The unit ends at the comma inside 219.

sentences.t: πόθεσαν δ’ ἥρωες Ἀχαιοί.
sentences.tr: pothesan d’ hērōes Achaioi.
sentences.l: and the hero Achaeans missed him.
sentences.i: and the Achaean heroes missed him.
sentences.n: πόθεσαν is the unaugmented aorist of ποθέω ‘long for, miss’, and the aorist says that they came to feel his loss. ἥρωες Ἀχαιοί is ‘the hero Achaeans’, the epithet kept as in the table.

sentences.t: καὶ τότ’ Ἀπόλλωνα προσέφη νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς·
sentences.tr: kai tot’ Apollōna prosephē nephelēgereta Zeus·
sentences.l: And then cloud-gatherer Zeus addressed Apollo:
sentences.i: Then Zeus who gathers the clouds spoke to Apollo:
sentences.n: Ἀπόλλωνα is the object of προσέφη ‘addressed’, and νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς ‘cloud-gatherer Zeus’ is the subject; νεφεληγερέτα is the epic nominative (Attic -ης).

sentences.t: ἔρχεο νῦν φίλε Φοῖβε μεθ’ Ἕκτορα χαλκοκορυστήν·
sentences.tr: ercheo nyn phile Phoibe meth’ Hektora chalkokorystēn·
sentences.l: “Go now, dear Phoebus, to Hector, bronze-armed;
sentences.i: “Go now, dear Phoebus, to Hector armed in bronze;
sentences.n: ἔρχεο is the epic imperative of ἔρχομαι ‘go’. Φοῖβε is the vocative of Φοῖβος, Apollo’s name Phoebus. μεθ’ Ἕκτορα ‘to Hector’ is μετά with the accusative, ‘to, after’. χαλκοκορυστήν ‘armed in bronze’ is the table’s rendering, from κορύσσω ‘arm’.

sentences.t:
ἤδη μὲν γάρ τοι γαιήοχος ἐννοσίγαιος
οἴχεται εἰς ἅλα δῖαν ἀλευάμενος χόλον αἰπὺν
ἡμέτερον·
sentences.tr:
ēdē men gar toi gaiēochos ennosigaios
oichetai eis hala dian aleuamenos cholon aipyn
hēmeteron·
sentences.i: For already the earth-holder, the earth-shaker, has gone off to the heavenly brine, avoiding our steep anger;
sentences.n: γαιήοχος ἐννοσίγαιος ‘the earth-holder, the earth-shaker’ is Poseidon, the two epithets standing for the name. οἴχεται is ‘has gone, is gone’. ἅλα δῖαν keeps δῖος ‘heavenly’ even of the sea. ἀλευάμενος is the aorist participle of ἀλέομαι ‘avoid’. χόλον αἰπύν ‘steep anger’ keeps αἰπύς as ‘steep’ wherever it stands; said of anger it is a figure, and the Greek does not say what it means. ἡμέτερον is the plural ‘our’, most naturally Zeus speaking of his own anger.

sentences.t:
μάλα γάρ κε μάχης ἐπύθοντο καὶ ἄλλοι,
οἵ περ ἐνέρτεροί εἰσι θεοὶ Κρόνον ἀμφὶς ἐόντες.
sentences.tr:
mala gar ke machēs epythonto kai alloi,
hoi per enerteroi eisi theoi Kronon amphis eontes.
sentences.l:
for very much would others too have learned of the fighting,
the gods who are lower, being about Cronus.
sentences.i: for others too would surely have heard of the fighting, even the gods who are lower down, around Cronus.
sentences.n: κε with ἐπύθοντο makes the aorist a past potential: ‘would have learned’. πυνθάνομαι takes the genitive μάχης. οἵ περ is ‘those who indeed’. ἐνέρτεροι is the comparative ‘lower, further below’, the old gods down below who are with Cronus; the Greek does not call them Titans here, but they are usually understood as the Titans of 14.279; ἀμφίς means ‘about, around’ and takes Κρόνον.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ τόδ’ ἠμὲν ἐμοὶ πολὺ κέρδιον ἠδέ οἱ αὐτῷ
ἔπλετο, ὅττι πάροιθε νεμεσσηθεὶς ὑπόειξε
χεῖρας ἐμάς,
sentences.tr:
alla tod’ ēmen emoi poly kerdion ēde hoi autōi
epleto, hotti paroithe nemessētheis hypoeixe
cheiras emas,
sentences.l:
But this both for me much better and for himself
was, that beforehand, having felt resentment, he yielded
to my hands,
sentences.i: But it was much better both for me and for himself that he gave way to my hands beforehand, though resentful,
sentences.n: ἠμὲν … ἠδέ is ‘both … and’. κέρδιον is ‘more profitable, better’, and ἔπλετο is the aorist ‘proved to be’. ὅττι is ὅτι ‘that’, and πάροιθε ‘beforehand’. νεμεσσηθείς ‘having felt resentment’ is as at 211. ὑπόειξε χεῖρας ἐμάς is ‘gave way before my hands’, with the accusative as the thing before which one gives way.

sentences.t: ἐπεὶ οὔ κεν ἀνιδρωτί γ’ ἐτελέσθη.
sentences.tr: epei ou ken anidrōti g’ etelesthē.
sentences.l: since not without sweat would it have been accomplished.
sentences.i: for it would not have been accomplished without sweat.
sentences.n: ἐπεὶ οὔ κεν … ἐτελέσθη is ‘since it would not have been accomplished’, the aorist with κε. ἀνιδρωτί ‘without sweat’ is an adverb, from ἱδρώς ‘sweat’ with the negative prefix. γ’ is the emphasising particle. The verb τελέω keeps ‘accomplish, fulfil’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σύ γ’ ἐν χείρεσσι λάβ’ αἰγίδα θυσσανόεσσαν,
τῇ μάλ’ ἐπισσείων φοβέειν ἥρωας Ἀχαιούς·
sentences.tr:
alla sy g’ en cheiressi lab’ aigida thyssanoessan,
tēi mal’ episseiōn phobeein hērōas Achaious·
sentences.l:
But you, in your hands take the tasselled aegis,
and shaking it hard frighten the hero Achaeans;
sentences.i: But you, take the tasselled aegis in your hands and shake it hard to frighten the Achaean heroes;
sentences.n: λάβ’ is λάβε, the aorist imperative of λαμβάνω ‘take’. θυσσανόεσσαν ‘tasselled’ is the table’s rendering. ἐπισσείων is the participle of ἐπισσείω ‘shake over’, and τῇ ‘with it’ is the aegis. φοβέειν is the epic infinitive of φοβέω ‘frighten’, used as an imperative like δέχεσθαι at 1.20.

sentences.t: σοὶ δ’ αὐτῷ μελέτω ἑκατηβόλε φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ·
sentences.tr: soi d’ autōi meletō hekatēbole phaidimos Hektōr·
sentences.l: and to you yourself let be a care, far-shooting one, glorious Hector;
sentences.i: and let glorious Hector be your own concern, you who shoot from afar;
sentences.n: μελέτω is the imperative of μέλω ‘be a care to’, with σοί … αὐτῷ ‘to you yourself’ in the dative. ἑκατηβόλε is the vocative of ἑκατηβόλος ‘far-shooting’, Apollo’s epithet. φαίδιμος ‘glorious’ is the table’s rendering.

sentences.t:
τόφρα γὰρ οὖν οἱ ἔγειρε μένος μέγα, ὄφρ’ ἂν Ἀχαιοὶ
φεύγοντες νῆάς τε καὶ Ἑλλήσποντον ἵκωνται.
sentences.tr:
tophra gar oun hoi egeire menos mega, ophr’ an Achaioi
pheugontes nēas te kai Hellēsponton hikōntai.
sentences.l:
for that long, then, rouse great might in him, until the Achaeans,
fleeing, come to the ships and the Hellespont;
sentences.i: For until the Achaeans, fleeing, reach the ships and the Hellespont, keep rousing great might in him;
sentences.n: τόφρα … ὄφρ’ ἂν ‘for as long … until’ pairs the two clauses; ὄφρα ἄν with the subjunctive ἵκωνται is ‘until they come’. ἔγειρε is the present imperative of ἐγείρω ‘rouse’, and οἱ is ‘in him’, Hector. μένος keeps ‘might’ in the Iliad. Ἑλλήσποντον ‘Hellespont’ is the strait beside which the ships lie.

sentences.t:
κεῖθεν δ’ αὐτὸς ἐγὼ φράσομαι ἔργον τε ἔπος τε,
ὥς κε καὶ αὖτις Ἀχαιοὶ ἀναπνεύσωσι πόνοιο.
sentences.tr:
keithen d’ autos egō phrasomai ergon te epos te,
hōs ke kai autis Achaioi anapneusōsi ponoio.
sentences.l:
and from there I myself will devise deed and word,
so that the Achaeans too may get their breath back again from toil.”
sentences.i: From that point I myself will plan both deed and word, so that the Achaeans too may get their breath back from their toil.”
sentences.n: κεῖθεν ‘from there’ means from the point where the Achaeans have reached the ships. φράσομαι is the future of φράζομαι ‘plan, devise’, and ἔργον τε ἔπος τε is ‘both deed and word’. ὥς κε … ἀναπνεύσωσι is a purpose clause in the subjunctive. ἀναπνέω is ‘breathe again’, and πόνοιο is the genitive ‘from toil’. Zeus’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, οὐδ’ ἄρα πατρὸς ἀνηκούστησεν Ἀπόλλων,
sentences.tr: hōs ephat’, oud’ ara patros anēkoustēsen Apollōn,
sentences.l: So he spoke, and not at all did Apollo fail to listen to his father,
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Apollo did not fail to listen to his father,
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ ‘so he spoke’. ἀνηκούστησεν is the aorist of ἀνηκουστέω ‘be unhearing, not listen’, built on ἀνήκουστος, with οὐδ’ ἄρα ‘and not at all’. The sense is that Apollo listened and obeyed. πατρός is the genitive that the verb takes. This line differs from the Odyssey’s οὐδ’ ἀπίθησε ‘did not disobey’, which is a different verb.

sentences.t:
βῆ δὲ κατ’ Ἰδαίων ὀρέων ἴρηκι ἐοικὼς
ὠκέϊ φασσοφόνῳ, ὅς τ’ ὤκιστος πετεηνῶν.
sentences.tr:
bē de kat’ Idaiōn oreōn irēki eoikōs
ōkeï phassophonōi, hos t’ ōkistos peteēnōn.
sentences.l:
and he went down from the Idaean mountains like a hawk,
swift, dove-slaying, which is the swiftest of winged creatures.
sentences.i: and he came down from the Idaean mountains in the likeness of a swift hawk, a killer of doves, the swiftest of all winged things.
sentences.n: βῆ is the unaugmented aorist of βαίνω ‘went’, and κατ’ with the genitive ὀρέων is ‘down from’. Ἰδαίων is the adjective ‘of Ida’. ἴρηκι ἐοικώς is ‘like a hawk’, ἐοικώς the perfect participle of ἔοικα with the dative. φασσοφόνῳ is ‘dove-slaying’, from φάσσα ‘dove’ and the root of φόνος. ὅς τ’ ὤκιστος is ‘which is the swiftest’, with the general τε, and πετεηνῶν the genitive ‘of winged things’.

sentences.t:
εὗρ’ υἱὸν Πριάμοιο δαΐφρονος Ἕκτορα δῖον
ἥμενον,
sentences.tr:
heur’ huion Priamoio daïphronos Hektora dion
hēmenon,
sentences.l:
He found the son of Priam, wise-minded, heavenly Hector,
sitting,
sentences.i: He found the son of wise-hearted Priam, heavenly Hector, sitting,
sentences.n: εὗρ’ is εὗρε ‘found’. υἱὸν Πριάμοιο δαΐφρονος Ἕκτορα δῖον is the line of 11.197 (where Iris finds Hector), with δαΐφρονος going with Πριάμοιο; whether the epithet means ‘wise’ or ‘fierce’ is disputed. ἥμενον is the participle of ἧμαι ‘sit’. The subject is Apollo, who had set out in the last line.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἔτι κεῖτο, νέον δ’ ἐσαγείρετο θυμόν,
ἀμφὶ ἓ γιγνώσκων ἑτάρους·
sentences.tr:
oud’ eti keito, neon d’ esageireto thymon,
amphi he gignōskōn hetarous·
sentences.l:
and no longer was he lying, and newly was gathering his spirit,
recognizing his comrades about him;
sentences.i: he was no longer lying down, and was just then gathering his spirit again, knowing his comrades around him;
sentences.n: οὐδ’ ἔτι κεῖτο ‘and no longer was he lying’; κεῖτο is the imperfect of κεῖμαι. νέον ‘newly, just now’. ἐσαγείρετο is the imperfect middle of ἐσαγείρω (εἰς + ἀγείρω ‘gather’), ‘was collecting into himself’, and θυμόν ‘spirit’ is the object. ἀμφὶ ἕ is ‘around himself’, with ἕ the reflexive. γιγνώσκων ‘recognizing’; ἑτάρους ‘comrades’ is the Homeric ἑταίρους.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ ἆσθμα καὶ ἱδρὼς
παύετ’, ἐπεί μιν ἔγειρε Διὸς νόος αἰγιόχοιο.
sentences.tr:
atar asthma kai hidrōs
pauet’, epei min egeire Dios noos aigiochoio.
sentences.l:
but gasping and sweat
were ceasing, since the mind of aegis-bearing Zeus was rousing him.
sentences.i: and his panting and sweat were stopping, because the mind of aegis-bearing Zeus was rousing him.
sentences.n: ἆσθμα is ‘panting, hard breathing’, and ἱδρώς ‘sweat’. παύετ’ is παύετο, the middle imperfect ‘was ceasing’. ἐπεί … ἔγειρε is ‘since … was rousing’, with the imperfect for a continuing effect. Διὸς νόος αἰγιόχοιο ‘the mind of aegis-bearing Zeus’ is the cause: Zeus’s will had begun to restore him. αἰγιόχοιο ‘aegis-bearing’ is the table’s epithet.

sentences.t: ἀγχοῦ δ’ ἱστάμενος προσέφη ἑκάεργος Ἀπόλλων·
sentences.tr: anchou d’ histamenos prosephē hekaergos Apollōn·
sentences.l: And standing close by addressed far-working Apollo:
sentences.i: Standing close beside him, Apollo, who works from afar, spoke to him:
sentences.n: ἀγχοῦ ‘close by’ with the participle ἱστάμενος ‘standing’; ἑκάεργος ‘far-working’ is Apollo’s epithet, rendered as the table has it, and the note in the Odyssey says its sense is disputed (‘far-shooting’ is the other guess).

sentences.t:
Ἕκτορ υἱὲ Πριάμοιο, τί ἢ δὲ σὺ νόσφιν ἀπ’ ἄλλων
ἧσ’ ὀλιγηπελέων;
sentences.tr:
Hektor huie Priamoio, ti ē de sy nosphin ap’ allōn
hēs’ oligēpeleōn;
sentences.l:
“Hector, son of Priam, why indeed do you, apart from the others,
sit faint with little strength?
sentences.i: “Hector, son of Priam, why are you sitting there faint, away from the others?
sentences.n: Ἕκτορ υἱὲ Πριάμοιο is a vocative with a genitive of the father. τί ἢ δέ is ‘why then’. νόσφιν ἀπ’ ἄλλων is ‘apart from the others’. ἧσ’ is ἧσο, the second person imperfect of ἧμαι ‘you sit’. ὀλιγηπελέων is ‘faint’ (‘faint with little strength’ word for word), the Odyssey’s rendering of the same participle.

sentences.t: ἦ πού τί σε κῆδος ἱκάνει;
sentences.tr: ē pou ti se kēdos hikanei;
sentences.l: Can it be that some trouble comes upon you?”
sentences.i: Can it be that some trouble has come upon you?”
sentences.n: ἦ πού is ‘can it be that, I suppose’, a question that expects trouble. κῆδος is ‘trouble, care’, and σε is the object of ἱκάνει ‘comes upon’. Apollo’s question ends here, and Hector answers.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ὀλιγοδρανέων προσέφη κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ·
sentences.tr: ton d’ oligodraneōn prosephē korythaiolos Hektōr·
sentences.l: Him, weak, addressed Hector of the glancing helmet:
sentences.i: Weak as he was, Hector of the glancing helmet said to him:
sentences.n: ὀλιγοδρανέων is the participle of ὀλιγοδρανέω ‘be feeble’, built on ὀλίγος ‘little’; its meaning is ‘feeble, with little strength’, and it is a near relative of ὀλιγηπελέων in 245. κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ ‘Hector of the glancing helmet’ is the table’s epithet. The verb is προσέφη ‘addressed’.

sentences.t: τίς δὲ σύ ἐσσι φέριστε θεῶν ὅς μ’ εἴρεαι ἄντην;
sentences.tr: tis de sy essi pheriste theōn hos m’ eireai antēn;
sentences.l: “And who are you, best of the gods, who ask me to my face?
sentences.i: “And who are you, best of the gods, who ask me to my face?
sentences.n: τίς δὲ σύ ἐσσι is ‘and who are you’; ἐσσι is the epic second person of εἰμί. φέριστε is the vocative of the superlative φέριστος ‘best’, here ‘best of the gods’, as it is ‘best of men’ in the Odyssey. θεῶν is the partitive genitive. εἴρεαι is the second person of εἴρομαι ‘ask’, and ἄντην ‘face to face’ is an adverb.

sentences.l:
Do you not hear that me, at the hindmost ships of the Achaeans,
as I was destroying his comrades, Ajax, good at the war-cry, struck
with a stone on the chest, and made me cease from impetuous might?
sentences.i: Do you not hear how, by the hindmost ships of the Achaeans, as I was destroying his comrades, Ajax, good at the war-cry, struck me on the chest with a stone and stopped me from my impetuous might?
sentences.n: ἀΐεις is ‘you hear, perceive’. ὅ is the old neuter ὅτι ‘that’. νηυσὶν ἔπι πρυμνῇσιν is ‘by the hindmost ships’, πρυμνός being the adjective from πρύμνη ‘stern’. οὓς ἑτάρους ‘his comrades’ has ὅς in its possessive sense, Ajax’s own, which is to be told apart from the relative. ὀλέκοντα ‘destroying’ agrees with με, the object of βάλεν ‘struck’. βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Αἴας ‘Ajax, good at the war-cry’ is the stock phrase. χερμαδίῳ is the dative ‘with a stone’. θούριδος ἀλκῆς ‘impetuous might’ is in the genitive after ἔπαυσε ‘stopped’.

sentences.t:
καὶ δὴ ἔγωγ’ ἐφάμην νέκυας καὶ δῶμ’ Ἀΐδαο
ἤματι τῷδ’ ἵξεσθαι, ἐπεὶ φίλον ἄϊον ἦτορ.
sentences.tr:
kai dē egōg’ ephamēn nekyas kai dōm’ Aïdao
ēmati tōid’ hixesthai, epei philon aïon ētor.
sentences.l:
Why, I thought that I would come to the dead and the house of Hades
on this day, since I was breathing out my dear heart.”
sentences.i: I thought I would reach the dead and the house of Hades this very day, since I was breathing out my dear heart.”
sentences.n: καὶ δή ‘why, indeed’. ἐφάμην is the imperfect of φημί, ‘I thought’. νέκυας is the accusative plural of νέκυς ‘dead one’, and Ἀΐδαο is the epic genitive of Ἅιδης. ἵξεσθαι is the future infinitive of ἱκνέομαι ‘come to’. ἄϊον is taken as the imperfect of a second ἀΐω, ‘breathe out, gasp’, which fits the sense: it is not the ἀΐω ‘hear’ of 248. ἦτορ ‘heart’ is the life breathed out. Hector’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπεν ἄναξ ἑκάεργος Ἀπόλλων·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipen anax hekaergos Apollōn·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed lord far-working Apollo:
sentences.i: Then lord Apollo, who works from afar, spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπεν is the formula as at 205, here with ἄναξ ἑκάεργος Ἀπόλλων ‘lord far-working Apollo’; ἄναξ ‘lord’ keeps the table’s rendering. προσέειπεν is the epic προσεῖπεν.

sentences.t: θάρσει νῦν·
sentences.tr: tharsei nyn·
sentences.l: “Take courage now;
sentences.i: “Take heart now;
sentences.n: θάρσει is the imperative of θαρσέω ‘take courage’. νῦν ‘now’.

sentences.t:
τοῖόν τοι ἀοσσητῆρα Κρονίων
ἐξ Ἴδης προέηκε παρεστάμεναι καὶ ἀμύνειν
Φοῖβον Ἀπόλλωνα χρυσάορον,
sentences.tr:
toion toi aossētēra Kroniōn
ex Idēs proeēke parestamenai kai amynein
Phoibon Apollōna chrysaoron,
sentences.i: The son of Cronus has sent from Ida such a helper for you, to stand by and ward off: Phoebus Apollo of the golden sword,
sentences.n: τοῖον … ἀοσσητῆρα ‘such a helper’, with τοι ‘for you’. Κρονίων ‘the son of Cronus’ is Zeus. προέηκε is the aorist of προίημι ‘send forth’, and the infinitives παρεστάμεναι ‘to stand beside’ and ἀμύνειν ‘to ward off’ give the purpose. Φοῖβον Ἀπόλλωνα is the accusative in apposition to ἀοσσητῆρα: the god is speaking of himself in the third person. χρυσάορον is ‘of the golden sword’, from χρυσός ‘gold’ and ἄορ ‘sword’; the second half is taken as ‘sword’, but the compound’s sense is not certain.

sentences.t:
ὅς σε πάρος περ
ῥύομ’, ὁμῶς αὐτόν τε καὶ αἰπεινὸν πτολίεθρον.
sentences.tr:
hos se paros per
rhyom’, homōs auton te kai aipeinon ptoliethron.
sentences.l:
who even before protect you,
alike yourself and the steep citadel.
sentences.i: I, who have protected you till now, you yourself and your steep citadel alike.
sentences.n: ὅς σε … ῥύομ’ is ‘who protect you’: ῥύομ’ is ῥύομαι, a first person form, so the relative clause turns from third person to first, as Apollo speaks of himself. πάρος περ ‘even before, until now’. ὁμῶς … τε καὶ is ‘alike … and’, with αὐτόν ‘yourself’ and αἰπεινὸν πτολίεθρον ‘the steep citadel’ both objects.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε νῦν ἱππεῦσιν ἐπότρυνον πολέεσσι
νηυσὶν ἔπι γλαφυρῇσιν ἐλαυνέμεν ὠκέας ἵππους·
sentences.tr:
all’ age nyn hippeusin epotrynon poleessi
nēusin epi glaphyrēisin elaunemen ōkeas hippous·
sentences.l:
But come now, urge on the many horsemen
to drive their swift horses at the hollow ships;
sentences.i: But come now, urge your many horsemen to drive their swift horses at the hollow ships;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε νῦν ‘but come now’. ἐπότρυνον is the aorist imperative of ἐποτρύνω ‘urge on’, and ἱππεῦσιν πολέεσσι is the dative plural ‘many horsemen’. ἐλαυνέμεν is the epic infinitive of ἐλαύνω ‘drive’. νηυσὶν ἔπι γλαφυρῇσιν is ‘at the hollow ships’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ προπάροιθε κιὼν ἵπποισι κέλευθον
πᾶσαν λειανέω, τρέψω δ’ ἥρωας Ἀχαιούς.
sentences.tr:
autar egō proparoithe kiōn hippoisi keleuthon
pasan leianeō, trepsō d’ hērōas Achaious.
sentences.l:
and I, going before, the whole way for the horses
will make smooth, and will turn the hero Achaeans.”
sentences.i: and I, going before them, will level the whole way for the horses, and turn the Achaean heroes back.”
sentences.n: προπάροιθε κιών is ‘going before’, κιών being the participle of κίω ‘go’. λειανέω is the future of λειαίνω ‘make smooth’, and κέλευθον … πᾶσαν ‘the whole way’ is its object. ἵπποισι is the dative ‘for the horses’. τρέψω is ‘I will turn’, and the turning is to flight. Apollo’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν ἔμπνευσε μένος μέγα ποιμένι λαῶν.
sentences.tr: hōs eipōn empneuse menos mega poimeni laōn.
sentences.l: So having spoken, he breathed great might into the shepherd of the people.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and breathed great might into the shepherd of the people.
sentences.n: ἔμπνευσε is the aorist of ἐμπνέω ‘breathe into’. μένος μέγα ‘great might’; ποιμένι λαῶν ‘shepherd of the people’ is Hector, left unnamed.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτε τις στατὸς ἵππος ἀκοστήσας ἐπὶ φάτνῃ
δεσμὸν ἀπορρήξας θείῃ πεδίοιο κροαίνων
εἰωθὼς λούεσθαι ἐϋρρεῖος ποταμοῖο
κυδιόων·
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hote tis statos hippos akostēsas epi phatnēi
desmon aporrēxas theiēi pedioio kroainōn
eiōthōs louesthai eÿrreios potamoio
kydioōn·
sentences.l:
And as when some stalled horse, fed on barley at the manger,
having broken the tether, may run over the plain, pounding,
accustomed to bathe in the fair-flowing river,
glorying;
sentences.i: As when some stalled horse, fed on barley at the manger, breaks his tether and runs pounding over the plain, accustomed to bathe in the fair-flowing river, glorying;
sentences.n: The simile is the one that stands for Paris at 6.506–511, here with Hector. ὡς δ’ ὅτε τις ‘and as when some’; στατὸς ἵππος is a horse kept at the stall. ἀκοστήσας is a rare aorist participle from ἀκοστή ‘barley’, ‘fed on barley’. ἀπορρήξας is the aorist participle ‘having broken’, and θείῃ is the subjunctive of θέω ‘run’, in the general ‘as when … he may run’. κροαίνων ‘pounding’ is of the hooves. εἰωθώς ‘accustomed’ is the perfect participle, and ἐϋρρεῖος ποταμοῖο is ‘of the fair-flowing river’. κυδιόων ‘glorying’ ends the unit at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
ὑψοῦ δὲ κάρη ἔχει, ἀμφὶ δὲ χαῖται
ὤμοις ἀΐσσονται·
sentences.tr:
hypsou de karē echei, amphi de chaitai
ōmois aïssontai·
sentences.l:
and high he holds his head, and about
his shoulders the mane streams;
sentences.i: he holds his head high, and his mane streams about his shoulders;
sentences.n: The horse as he runs. ὑψοῦ δὲ κάρη ἔχει ‘and he holds his head high’; ἀμφὶ δὲ … ὤμοις ‘and about his shoulders’, the dative after ἀμφί. χαῖται is the plural of χαίτη ‘mane’, and ἀΐσσονται is ‘dart, stream’, a present middle in the plural to agree with it.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἀγλαΐηφι πεποιθὼς
ῥίμφά ἑ γοῦνα φέρει μετά τ’ ἤθεα καὶ νομὸν ἵππων·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ aglaïēphi pepoithōs
rhimpha he gouna pherei meta t’ ēthea kai nomon hippōn·
sentences.l:
and he, trusting in his splendour,
lightly his knees carry him to the haunts and pasture of the horses;
sentences.i: and, trusting in his beauty, his knees carry him lightly to the haunts and pasture of the horses;
sentences.n: ὃ δέ ‘and he’ is the horse. ἀγλαΐηφι is the dative with the ending -φι (the instrumental), ‘in his splendour’, and πεποιθώς is the perfect participle ‘trusting’. ῥίμφα ‘lightly’ is the adverb, with ἕ ‘him’ as the object of φέρει ‘carries’. ἤθεα ‘haunts’ and νομόν ‘pasture’ are the places he runs to; the genitive ἵππων says whose they are.

sentences.t:
ὣς Ἕκτωρ λαιψηρὰ πόδας καὶ γούνατ’ ἐνώμα
ὀτρύνων ἱππῆας, ἐπεὶ θεοῦ ἔκλυεν αὐδήν.
sentences.tr:
hōs Hektōr laipsēra podas kai gounat’ enōma
otrynōn hippēas, epei theou eklyen audēn.
sentences.l:
So Hector quickly his feet and knees set moving,
urging on the horsemen, since he heard the voice of the god.
sentences.i: So Hector set his feet and knees moving quickly, urging on the horsemen, since he had heard the god’s voice.
sentences.n: ὣς Ἕκτωρ closes the simile. λαιψηρά ‘quickly’ is the neuter plural used as an adverb, and ἐνώμα is the imperfect of νωμάω ‘ply, move’, with πόδας καὶ γούνατ’ ‘feet and knees’ as its object; γούνατ’ is γούνατα, the epic plural of γόνυ. ὀτρύνων ‘urging on’, and ἱππῆας ‘horsemen’ is the Homeric ἱππέας. ἔκλυεν is the aorist of κλύω ‘hear’, with the genitive θεοῦ and αὐδήν ‘voice’.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ὥς τ’ ἢ ἔλαφον κεραὸν ἢ ἄγριον αἶγα
ἐσσεύαντο κύνες τε καὶ ἀνέρες ἀγροιῶται·
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ hōs t’ ē elaphon keraon ē agrion aiga
esseuanto kynes te kai aneres agroiōtai·
sentences.l:
And they, as when either a horned stag or a wild goat
dogs and men, countrymen, have driven off:
sentences.i: And as when dogs and countrymen drive off a horned stag or a wild goat:
sentences.n: A second simile. οἳ δ’ ὥς τε is ‘and they, as when’; the Greek does not name those who are ‘they’, and the Danaans come in only at 277. ἢ … ἢ is ‘either … or’, and ἔλαφον κεραόν is ‘a horned stag’ (κεραός is from κέρας ‘horn’). ἐσσεύαντο is the aorist of a simile, as at 11.549: it states what happens each time, and the English uses the present. ἀνέρες ἀγροιῶται ‘countrymen’ are the men of the farms.

sentences.t:
τὸν μέν τ’ ἠλίβατος πέτρη καὶ δάσκιος ὕλη
εἰρύσατ’, οὐδ’ ἄρα τέ σφι κιχήμεναι αἴσιμον ἦεν·
sentences.tr:
ton men t’ ēlibatos petrē kai daskios hylē
eirysat’, oud’ ara te sphi kichēmenai aisimon ēen·
sentences.l:
that one a towering rock and shady wood
guarded, and not at all for them to overtake was it fitting;
sentences.i: a towering rock and a shady wood guard it, and it is not their lot to overtake it;
sentences.n: τόν is ‘that one’, the stag or goat. ἠλίβατος ‘towering’ is the Odyssey’s rendering of an adjective whose meaning is not known, and δάσκιος is ‘deeply shaded’, a compound of the intensive δα- and σκιά ‘shade’. εἰρύσατ’ is the aorist of ἐρύομαι ‘guard’, in a simile’s timeless sense. κιχήμεναι is the epic infinitive of κιχάνω ‘overtake’, and αἴσιμον ἦεν ‘was fitting, was allotted’ takes it; σφι is ‘for them’.

sentences.t:
τῶν δέ θ’ ὑπὸ ἰαχῆς ἐφάνη λὶς ἠϋγένειος
εἰς ὁδόν, αἶψα δὲ πάντας ἀπέτραπε καὶ μεμαῶτας·
sentences.tr:
tōn de th’ hypo iachēs ephanē lis ēÿgeneios
eis hodon, aipsa de pantas apetrape kai memaōtas·
sentences.l:
and at their shouting there appeared a fine-bearded lion
into the way, and at once turned all away, though eager;
sentences.i: and at their shouting a fine-bearded lion appears in the road and turns them all back at once, eager though they are;
sentences.n: τῶν δέ θ’ ὑπὸ ἰαχῆς is ‘and at their shouting’, the hunters’. ἐφάνη is the aorist passive of φαίνω, ‘appeared’, in a simile’s timeless sense. λίς is ‘lion’, a poetic word, and ἠϋγένειος ‘fine-bearded’ is the edition’s spelling with the diaeresis. εἰς ὁδόν is ‘into the way’. ἀπέτραπε is ‘turned away’, with πάντας as object, and μεμαῶτας ‘eager’ is the perfect participle, in the accusative to agree with it.

sentences.t:
ὣς Δαναοὶ εἷος μὲν ὁμιλαδὸν αἰὲν ἕποντο
νύσσοντες ξίφεσίν τε καὶ ἔγχεσιν ἀμφιγύοισιν·
sentences.tr:
hōs Danaoi heios men homiladon aien heponto
nyssontes xiphesin te kai enchesin amphigyoisin·
sentences.l:
So the Danaans, while in a throng they continually followed,
stabbing with swords and with double-pointed spears;
sentences.i: So the Danaans, for as long as they kept following in a throng, stabbing with swords and double-pointed spears,
sentences.n: ὣς Δαναοί ‘so the Danaans’ returns to the narrative. εἷος μέν is ‘for as long as’, matched by the αὐτὰρ ἐπεί of the next line. ὁμιλαδόν ‘in a throng’; ἕποντο is the unaugmented imperfect of ἕπομαι ‘follow’. νύσσοντες is ‘stabbing’, with ξίφεσιν ‘swords’ and ἔγχεσιν ἀμφιγύοισιν ‘with double-pointed spears’ in the dative of means; ἀμφιγύοισιν is the Odyssey’s rendering of a word of uncertain meaning.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ ἴδον Ἕκτορ’ ἐποιχόμενον στίχας ἀνδρῶν
τάρβησαν, πᾶσιν δὲ παραὶ ποσὶ κάππεσε θυμός.
sentences.tr:
autar epei idon Hektor’ epoichomenon stichas andrōn
tarbēsan, pasin de parai posi kappese thymos.
sentences.l:
but when they saw Hector going along the ranks of men,
they were afraid, and in all, at their feet, fell the spirit.
sentences.i: but when they saw Hector going along the ranks of men, they were afraid, and the spirit of every man fell to his feet.
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ‘but when’ answers εἷος μέν. ἴδον is the unaugmented aorist of ὁράω ‘saw’. ἐποιχόμενον is the participle of ἐποίχομαι ‘go along, advance on’, and στίχας ἀνδρῶν ‘ranks of men’ is its object. τάρβησαν is the aorist of ταρβέω ‘be afraid’. πᾶσιν is ‘in all’, with παραὶ ποσί ‘at their feet’; κάππεσε is κατέπεσε, ‘fell down’, the -π- doubled by assimilation.
